analysis.one_liner: Bans forced-arbitration clauses and class-action bans in private student loan contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 15 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote in the House, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Private student loan contracts commonly require borrowers to settle any dispute in private arbitration instead of court, and to give up the right to join a class action. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable for private education loans, restoring borrowers' access to court and to class lawsuits, and it would let a court — not an arbitrator — decide whether the law applies. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People borrowing private student loans from banks and specialty lenders. They would keep the right to sue in court over servicing errors, overcharges, or collections abuse, and to join class actions that mandatory arbitration clauses currently block.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes any predispute arbitration agreement in a private education loan unenforceable, so lenders could no longer require borrowers to give up their day in court as a condition of getting the loan.

It also voids predispute joint-action waivers, which stop borrowers from banding together in class or collective actions — the main practical tool for challenging widespread misconduct affecting many borrowers at once.

It requires that a court, rather than an arbitrator, decide whether the ban applies, closing a common tactic in which the arbitration clause itself sends the question of its validity to the arbitrator.
The bill would not apply to arbitration provisions in labor union contracts, and it takes effect for disputes that arise after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders — banks, credit unions, and companies like Sallie Mae — would lose their ability to channel disputes into a private forum that generally favors the contract drafter, and would face more exposure to class litigation over servicing and collection practices. That cost could be partly passed to borrowers through pricing.

drawbacks.text: Costs could shift to borrowers: lenders facing more courtroom and class-action exposure might price loans higher or lend less freely, especially to riskier students.

Individual arbitration can be faster and cheaper for a single borrower than a lawsuit, and critics of banning arbitration note that most borrowers never litigate either way, so the practical benefit may accrue mainly to class-action lawyers in the cases where one is viable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but narrow: arbitration and class-waiver clauses matter most when a lender's misconduct touches many borrowers at once, since no individual borrower can afford to sue alone. The main cost — possible credit tightening or higher rates — is speculative and could be limited by competition. On balance, restoring legal recourse for a heavily indebted group outweighs the lender-side costs, though the bill would do nothing for the far larger population of federal loan borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill on February 11, 2021, with 11 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill's complete action history contains only two entries — introduction and referral to committee — meaning it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
Fifteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and any bill not passed by both chambers dies and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders, who keep their contractual right to force borrowers into arbitration and block class actions.

for.name: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar forced arbitration and class-action waivers in private education loans.

for.name: 15 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the House Judiciary chair and other Judiciary members.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress, leaving it without any path to a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported it; with no recorded votes, the partisan shape beyond that is unknown.

industries.note: Lenders rely on predispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers to keep loan disputes out of court and out of class actions, where systemic servicing and collection abuses are most effectively challenged. The bill would strip that shield, and lenders' interest in keeping it runs directly against borrowers' access to legal recourse.

Firms that administer consumer arbitration would lose a stream of education-loan disputes if lenders can no longer require arbitration. Borrowers generally fare better in court, so the providers' interest sits against the public's here.
